The thing about sitting down to write a thousand words with no particular prompt beyond “whatever comes to you” is that the freedom is as daunting as any strict assignment. The blank page feels like an invitation and a dare at once. An empty canvas in the mind fills quickly with the ghosts of conversations you didn't have, with half-remembered scents, with the memory of a dream in which you walked through a forest of books and the trees were whispering the endings of stories you hadn't read. The hum of the refrigerator in the next room becomes the soundtrack, the coffee cup on the table a sort of talisman. The sunlight slides across the wall in a way that makes you aware of the passage of time, which suddenly seems to shorten, as if 1000 words were a cliff you're speeding towards. But then the words begin to come, some slowly, some like water in spring, and the fear of emptiness recedes like a tide.

I think of my grandmother's kitchen, the way the light caught the flour she tossed in the air as she kneaded dough. There was a rhythm to it, the push and fold, the way her hands, spotted with age, moved with the confidence of having done this ten thousand times. The radio played softly in the background, some scratchy tune from the 50s, and she sang along off-key, her voice another ingredient in the bread. That smell — yeasty, warm, alive — remains one of the most comforting sensory memories I have. It makes me think about how smell is tied to emotion, how the neural pathways of scent carve deep grooves in the brain's landscapes. They say olfaction is the oldest sense, located close to the parts of the brain that process memory and emotion. A whiff of lilac can take you back decades in an instant.

There is a blue notebook somewhere with the beginnings of an unfinished story about a boy who found a key that opened nothing in his house but fitted perfectly into a crack in an old tree in the park. He turned it and found a voice, small and insistent, telling him secrets about the squirrels and the worms. He thought he was dreaming until he went back the next day and found the crack had grown into a door. I was twelve when I wrote that, convinced that magic lived just out of sight, if only you had the right talisman. I think now about the keys we carry — the experiences, the bits of knowledge, the empathy — and the doors they open in others.

If you asked me to list all the things that occupy my thoughts in a day, the list would be a mosaic: worry about deadlines, the desire to call old friends, the annoyance at the sound of my upstairs neighbor's squeaky floors, a fascination with the mating habits of octopuses (did you know they sometimes carry around shells for shelter?), a sudden urge to bake banana bread, the fear of missing out on life while scrolling endlessly through glowing rectangles. I think about time, about how our perception of it changes. How summer as a child stretched out like an eternity, the days slow and humid, filled with the endless possibility of fireflies and late-night games of hide-and-seek. How now weeks slip by in a blur, and you find yourself thinking, wasn't it just yesterday that I put away the winter coats?

To write whatever comes is to watch the mind at work, to be both actor and audience. It is to notice how one thought leads to another, sometimes logically, sometimes by leaps that would make no sense if diagrammed. This morning's breakfast of oatmeal reminds me of the instant oatmeal packets with dinosaurs in them, which in turn makes me think of a documentary I watched about how actual dinosaur fossils sometimes show traces of feathers, which brings to mind a poem by W. S. Merwin in which he imagines a future where all that is left of us will be some scattering of feathers. Birds are living dinosaurs, and there is something wonderful about the idea that the ancient world is still with us in the form of the sparrows hopping outside my window.

Language itself is a miraculous technology. Symbols on a page convey thought, emotion, entire worlds. We are pattern-seeking creatures; we string sounds together and imbue them with meaning, and somehow, across time and distance, someone else hears those sounds or reads those marks and something lights up in their brain, some recognition, some resonance. I was reading about how octopuses have a distributed nervous system; two-thirds of their neurons are in their arms. They can think with their limbs. Imagine writing if our hands had minds of their own, if our fingers could decide to compose a poem while we were busy thinking about grocery lists. Perhaps they do, in a way; sometimes the writing knows more than the writer.

The city outside is a collage of sirens, birds, car horns, and the hum of an air conditioner that never seems to stop. There is a lone tree on the sidewalk, planted in a square of dirt encircled by iron. Its leaves make a sound like whispered paper when the breeze is just right. People pass by it without looking, eyes on their phones, hearts somewhere else. Sometimes I stop and touch its bark, a small act of acknowledgment. The city trees work so hard for so little thanks. They filter air, provide shade, house birds, and yet they are often the most ignored members of the urban ecosystem.

What else comes? The memory of learning to ride a bicycle, knees scraped, the taste of blood and asphalt, the thrill of balance achieved, hands off the handlebars, a brief flight. The first time I saw the ocean, its vastness both terrifying and exhilarating, the way it seemed to breathe, waves inhaling and exhaling, foam like the lace trim on a giant's dress. The way the tide pulled at my ankles, a gentle insistence that I join it in its endless dance. I think of those who live by the sea, who measure time by tides instead of clocks.

There is also the darker stuff: the fear that all this — this writing, this thinking — is a way to avoid something more essential, the nagging voice that asks, to what end? The world is burning in places; people are suffering. Words seem like such a small tool. And yet, stories have changed minds, have ignited movements, have comforted the grieving. A letter can make someone's day; a poem can crack open a heart. We are narrative creatures; we understand ourselves through the stories we tell. Perhaps then, writing is not avoidance but engagement, a way of making sense, of connecting.

I can feel the word count creeping up. It's like watching the fuel gauge on a car descend as you drive through an empty stretch of desert. There is something freeing in knowing there's an end coming; constraints can be liberating. Nine hundred words, give or take. Time to land this plane, to bring the wandering thread back to something like coherence. Or maybe not. Maybe the beauty of "whatever comes" is that it doesn't have to resolve neatly. Life rarely does. It is a series of moments, linked by the fact that we perceive them in a line. Perhaps the act of writing them down, of catching them like fireflies in a jar, is enough. The jar glows, for a while. Then the light fades, the words remain, and we move on to the next blank page.
